A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TAIL research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments on 18 synthetic tasks, component ablations, data-proportion experiments, attention visualizations, and cross-task generalization results.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds token-usage results, a DeepSeek-R1 distillation comparison, and a reasoning-trace case study.

M1.justification: Both versions use Linear Transition, Atomic State, and Memory Fetcher to construct program-generated CoT training data. v2 clarifies Python implementation and loop-free atomic steps, but does not establish a changed algorithm, architecture, training objective, or inference procedure.

E1.justification: The task tables retain the same 18 tasks across eight algorithm classes, and the task-length tables retain their ranges. v1's appendix references to 28 tasks are corrected, not evidence of removed tasks. The added token-length and trace analyses concern existing Compare Numbers and Word Flip tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds R1-Distill-Qwen2.5-7B as a comparator in Table J1, describing fine-tuning with an equal amount of correctly distilled DeepSeek-R1 data. The comparator sets in Figure 3 and the Index Hint/Reversed Format comparison in Table 1 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The main text changes most-task training from 2–5 epochs to two and replaces per-task sample counts with 100,000 training and 500 evaluation examples per length range. v2 also introduces average CoT tokens and an equal-data distillation control. Appendix B still lists smaller sample-count exceptions, so these are reported setting changes without establishing reruns or fully resolving the actual sample sizes.

E4.justification: Appendix I adds an analysis of whether TAIL's accuracy advantage requires longer CoTs, and Appendix K adds a Word Flip reasoning-trace/error case study. The component/style ablations, data-mixture study, attention analysis, and cross-task generalization study already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new average-token metric does not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain their numerical results. New Table I1 reports 1,455 versus 1,461 average tokens and 90.0 versus 51.2 accuracy for TAIL versus DeepSeek-R1 on Compare Numbers. Table J1 adds S/M/L accuracies of 98.0/94.2/90.0 versus 72.2/67.2/61.8 for TAIL versus the distillation comparator, although it does not identify the task. These are added comparisons, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 6's explicit n!-enumeration/O(n!) complexity argument explaining inference-length constraints. The Turing-machine tuple and transition definitions remain, with full symbol definitions relocated to Appendix A. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: Both versions present the same central contributions: a general Turing-inspired CoT construction framework, three essential components, length generalization across 18 tasks, and performance exceeding prior methods and DeepSeek-R1. The added comparisons principally support and interpret these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 develops a structured-execution versus heuristic-exploration explanation and interprets comparable token usage as evidence of efficiency. Section 6 and Appendix L add limitations concerning closed-source models and nondeterministic/open-ended problems. Conversely, v1's detailed maximum-token, latency, memory, and factorial-scaling limitation is removed; Appendix I retains only a general CoT-growth concern. The cross-task transfer limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents manually written Python programs, string concatenation for both CoT styles, more than 20 query templates per task, and that displayed component tags are absent from actual CoT data. These clarify existing implementation. It omits v1's explicit statement that deduplication also removes identical operands under differently worded queries.

R1.justification: v2 removes the entire Eliciting Chain-of-Thought subsection and its prompting, SFT, and reinforcement-learning literature, including ReAct, the CoT Collection, and Satori. It adds works on the Chomsky hierarchy, programmable looped transformers, and CoT granularity. This substantially changes literature coverage, while retaining the direct positioning against Hou et al.'s Turing-program approach.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from before the preliminaries to after the experiments; Discussion becomes Limitations; and the conclusion and substantial experimental/method explanations are rewritten. CoT styles and inconsistent module terminology are revised, and existing appendix material is reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are substantially redrawn, existing result plots receive revised axes, colors, legends, and sizing, and the document adopts a different typography and page layout. v2 adds synthesis and Memory Fetcher diagrams plus Tables I1 and J1, while relocating and reformatting existing appendix displays.

improvement.justification: The added same-backbone distillation control and token-usage analysis address gaps in v1's comparisons, while Appendix C makes data generation easier to reconstruct. These provide a limited net improvement in clarity and empirical support. The gains are tempered by Table J1's unspecified task and sparse protocol details, unresolved sample-count inconsistencies, and removal of v1's concrete inference-cost limitation.
